questions.q: In the Gattermann aldehyde synthesis, benzene is treated with HCN, HCl and AlCl₃. The species formed before water is added is:
questions.explain: The iminium-type electrophile H–C⁺=NH substitutes the ring to give the aldimine, held as its hydrochloride in the acidic mixture; hydrolysis then gives benzaldehyde and NH₄⁺.

questions.q: Which substrate can be formylated by the Gattermann (HCN/HCl) method but NOT by the Gattermann–Koch (CO/HCl) method?
questions.explain: The HCN version works well on electron-rich phenols and phenol ethers, which the Gattermann–Koch reaction cannot handle. Nitrobenzene and benzonitrile are deactivated and fail in both.

questions.q: When Zn(CN)₂ and HCl are used in place of HCN, the zinc compound serves to:
options: reduce the aldimine to an amine
act as the hydrolysing agent in the second step
generate HCN in the flask and supply ZnCl₂ as the Lewis acid catalyst
questions.explain: Solid Zn(CN)₂ is safer than gaseous HCN; with HCl it gives HCN in situ, and the ZnCl₂ formed is the Lewis acid. Mesitylene is formylated to mesitaldehyde this way.

questions.q: In the closely related Houben–Hoesch reaction, a nitrile R–C≡N is used in place of H–C≡N. The final product after hydrolysis is:
questions.explain: Both reactions form an imine first and hydrolyse it at work-up; with R–C≡N the carbon carries R, so the product is Ar–CO–R, a ketone. H–C≡N gives the aldehyde.
